name: Avobenzone
lead: Avobenzone (butyl methoxydibenzoylmethane, trade name Parsol 1789) is an oil-soluble organic compound used as a UVA filter in chemical sunscreens and in moisturisers and cosmetics that carry an SPF claim [1][2]. It absorbs ultraviolet light across much of the UVA range, with an absorption peak near 357 nm [2].

How it helps appearance is through protection: UVA reaches deep into the skin and is associated with photoageing, so a filter that absorbs it is used to slow the lines, uneven tone and loss of firmness that accumulate with sun exposure. Dermatology sources describe daily sunscreen as a core anti-ageing step, and avobenzone is the UVA component of many US formulas [2][12].

It is notable for being the main UVA-absorbing organic filter permitted in the United States, at up to 3%, while the European Union permits up to 5% [2]. It is photounstable, losing absorbance under sunlight unless formulated with stabilisers such as octocrylene [1][2][3].

In 2019 and 2020, randomised trials sponsored by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) found that avobenzone and other sunscreen ingredients enter the bloodstream after topical use at concentrations above the 0.5 ng/mL threshold the agency had set for further safety study [4][5]. The authors and regulators stated that this finding does not by itself show that the ingredients are unsafe.

paras: Avobenzone is added to sunscreens, daytime moisturisers and makeup to absorb UVA radiation, which is associated with photoageing and skin cancer. FDA-listed products such as SPF 15 facial moisturisers combine it with homosalate, octisalate and octocrylene and carry label claims of helping prevent sunburn and decreasing the risk of skin cancer and early skin ageing when used with other sun protection measures [6]. Within looksmaxxing and skincare communities, sunscreen use is commonly discussed as an anti-ageing measure.

Wikipedia reports that avobenzone is the only UVA-absorbing organic filter FDA-approved in the US, at up to 3 percent, while the EU allows up to 5 percent and it is also approved in Australia and Japan [2]. A registered trial of UV and visible-light photoprotection in melasma enrolled 68 participants, reflecting interest in sunscreens for pigmentation [13]. A hydroquinone and retinol preparation containing sunscreens has also been tested for its sun protection strength [14].

Sun protection factor, a rating introduced in 1974 by the Austrian chemist Franz Greiter, describes protection against UVB, the wavelengths mainly responsible for sunburn. [22] UVA, at 315 to 400 nm, causes little reddening but reaches deeper into the skin, so broad-spectrum products add filters such as avobenzone to cover it. [22] US rules finalised in 2012 define broad spectrum as UVA protection proportional to UVB protection. [22] In the European Union, sunscreens are regulated as cosmetics and must meet minimum UVA requirements, including a UVA to UVB protection ratio of at least one third and a critical wavelength of at least 370 nm. [22]

Wikipedia's sunscreen article describes avobenzone as the notable organic filter that changes chemically under UV exposure and therefore usually needs a stabiliser in the formula. [22] In practice, products pair it with other organic filters or with newer photostable UVA filters, which is why ingredient lists on broad-spectrum sunscreens typically show avobenzone alongside octocrylene or similar partners. [2][3][6]

Avobenzone is a dibenzoylmethane derivative that exists mostly in the enol form and is insoluble in water [2]. Under sunlight its absorbance falls substantially; data cited by Wikipedia show a 36% drop after an hour of sun exposure [2]. Formulators therefore pair it with photostabilisers such as octocrylene, and studies of filter combinations have compared how well different mixtures retain their protection [3]. Mineral filters such as zinc oxide and titanium dioxide can accelerate its breakdown unless particles are coated [2].

Wikipedia notes that under UVA avobenzone can form a triplet excited state in its keto form, which can degrade the molecule, and that stabilisers include octocrylene, Tinosorb S and M, antioxidants such as vitamin E, and possibly cyclodextrin complexation [2]. A 2023 review describes drug-delivery strategies used to photostabilise avobenzone [15]. Avobenzone forms coloured complexes with iron(III) ions and can stain clothes in iron-rich water [2].

Wikipedia gives 1973 as the patent date, 1978 for approval in the EU and 1988 for FDA approval, with trade names including Parsol 1789 [2]. The FDA said in 2021 that it did not consider avobenzone generally recognised as safe and effective pending more data, and Palau banned it in 2020 over reef concerns [2].

Wikipedia's overview of sunscreen reports a 2013 Australian study of roughly 900 people in which those who applied broad-spectrum sunscreen daily for four and a half years showed smoother, more resilient skin than a control group, and a smaller study of 32 people in which daily SPF 30 use was associated with improvement in photoageing signs within 12 weeks. [22] These studies tested complete products rather than avobenzone alone.

Dermatology reviews describe photoprotection as the main preventive measure against photoageing, with sunscreens working alongside shade and clothing. [12][16] Avobenzone's role is to cover the UVA part of the spectrum, which is associated with photoageing changes in the dermis. [2][12]

In the United States sunscreens are regulated as over-the-counter drugs, a route that Wikipedia says has resulted in fewer approved filters than in the EU, where 29 were permitted as of 2023 against 17 in the US. [22] The FDA began sorting filters into categories of generally recognised as safe and effective, not recognised, or needing more data in 2019, and in a 2021 order only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide were placed in the first category. [22] Avobenzone remains widely sold in the US under the existing monograph while the agency's request for additional safety data is pending. [2]

A 2019 randomised trial under maximal-use conditions and a 2020 trial of six active ingredients, including avobenzone, oxybenzone, octocrylene, homosalate, octisalate and octinoxate, measured blood levels after sunscreen application and found systemic absorption [4][5]. A phase 1 registration of the same programme enrolled 72 participants [7]. These studies measured absorption, not clinical harm.

In 2021 the FDA said avobenzone was not currently classed as generally recognised as safe and effective, citing the need for more safety data, and Palau banned it in 2020 over reef concerns [2]. A 2017 laboratory study reported that chlorinated water and UV light can break avobenzone into other compounds [2]. UV filters in general have been detected in lake water and wastewater [8][9].

A 2025 review in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology states that FDA studies clearly demonstrate that organic UV filters are systemically absorbed during routine sunscreen use, while to date there is no evidence of associated negative health effects; it also reviews sunscreen and vitamin D, frontal fibrosing alopecia, benzene contamination and coral bleaching, where laboratory studies suggest organic filters are an additional contributing factor and several localities have banned certain filters [16]. Contact allergy to sunscreen ingredients has been described, including in a 1987 report on sensitivity to sunscreens and a European multicentre photopatch test study [17][18].

Human studies have mostly examined avobenzone as one ingredient among several in finished sunscreens. The 2019 and 2020 JAMA trials measured plasma concentrations and found systemic absorption [4][5]. A study of UVA exposure and singlet oxygen in skin (NCT05865431) enrolled 17 people [10], and a 2009 sunscreen SPF study in 10 participants is registered [11]. These do not test avobenzone alone for appearance outcomes.

A 1986 randomised trial examined a sunscreen containing butyl methoxydibenzoylmethane against UVA in photosensitised subjects [19]. A trial examined the capacity of sunscreens to protect people with lupus erythematosus in a photoprovocation test [20]. Analytical work developed a method to measure avobenzone and oxybenzone in human plasma for a sunscreen clinical trial [21].

timeline.event: JAMA maximal-use trial reports systemic absorption of sunscreen ingredients [5].
Second JAMA trial extends findings to six ingredients; Palau ban takes effect [4][2].
FDA states it does not consider avobenzone generally recognised as safe and effective pending more data [2].

card.summary: The main organic UVA filter in US sunscreens: widely used for photoageing protection, unstable in sunlight without stabilisers, absorbed into the bloodstream.
card.note: FDA says more safety data are needed; it is photounstable.

quick.overview:
Avobenzone is a chemical sunscreen filter that absorbs UVA light, the part of sunlight linked to photoageing. It is found in many sunscreens and SPF moisturisers.

It breaks down in sunlight unless paired with stabilisers like octocrylene. FDA-sponsored trials found it is absorbed into the blood after application.
quick.mechanism: Its conjugated structure absorbs UVA photons and releases the energy as heat, reducing UV reaching skin cells [1].
quick.risks: Regulators have asked for more safety data on systemic absorption; the studies measured blood levels, not harm. Allergy and environmental concerns have been reported, and Palau banned it in 2020 [2]. It is OTC; limits are 3% in the US and 5% in the EU.

chain: Absorbs UVA light in the sunscreen layer on the skin
Slower photoageing: fewer sun-related lines, spots and uneven tone
Skin that looks younger and more even over the years
angle.text: Avobenzone is an ingredient in sunscreens and SPF moisturisers that absorbs UVA, the part of sunlight linked to photoageing. People use it as part of a daily routine to protect skin appearance over time.
